To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we developed a noninvasive approach for the molecular classification of diffuse large B cell (DLBCL), the most common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and identified genomic patterns of clonal selection that distinguish indolent from aggressive lymphomas.

1. ctDNA analysis of DLBCL patients can classify transcriptionally-defined tumor subtypes and identify poor prognosis patients; 2. ctDNA analysis reveals patterns of clonality and clonal evolution in lymphomas that could facilitate prediction of histological transformations; 3. ctDNA analysis is predictive of clinical response to therapy and allows for noninvasive detection of minimal residual and emergent resistance mutations.
ctDNA profiling reveals molecular determinants of lymphoma clinical behavior.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of tumor DNA in the bloodstream.
the identification of biological factors underlying lymphoma clinical outcomes.
understanding the biology of cancer, and how this knowledge can be translated into improved clinical outcomes for cancer patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study has demonstrated the feasibility of using circulating tumor DNA to classify tumor subtypes and to track clonal evolution in lymphoma patients.
ctDNA analysis of lymphomas can reveal biological factors that underlies lymphoma clinical outcomes.
ctDNA analysis of DLBCL reveals distinct biological subtypes and allows classification of tumors based on cell of origin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that circulating tumor DNA is suitable for the noninvasive monitoring of minimal residual disease, and that ctDNA analysis can identify molecular factors that underlie tumor progression and may be useful for predicting patient outcome.
we have developed a new technology that can detect and monitor lymphomas in blood.
ctDNA analysis is a non-invasive method for the detection of residual disease, prediction of tumor evolution, and classification of tumor sub-types.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown that ctDNA analysis is a powerful tool to monitor lymphoma patients and to identify those who may benefit from additional treatment.
the amount of circulating tumor DNA in a patient’s blood is strongly associated with the aggressiveness of their cancer and can be used to identify poor-prognosis cases.
we can use the DNA that is shed by cancer cells into the blood to understand the biology of the tumor, and to predict how the tumor will behave.
